name: Mandarin
confidence_why: Duanmu 1990 and 2000, Dell 2004, Fon 2002, Huang 2004 and Yu and colleagues 2024 all treat Mandarin stress as lexical (which syllables are weak, neutral-toned, is fixed word by word, with no set position of main stress), while Dell 2004 rejects Duanmu's initial-prominent feet in favour of the right-edge prominence reported by Chao 1968 and Hoa 1983, so the position of stress among full syllables stays unsettled.

catalog_locator: Duanmu 2000 ms. sec. 4.1 (pp. 4-6) and sec. 4.4 (pp. 13-14); Duanmu 2011 sec. 3, exx. (5)-(7); Chao 1968:35,38 as carried by Duanmu
catalog_quote: It is well-known that stress in Chinese is hard to feel. ... Chao (1968: 35) suggests that in a string of full syllables, the last has most stress, the first has slightly less, and the rest have still less. This is known as the ‘medium-light-heavy’ theory. However, as Chao (1968: 38) acknowledges, Mandarin speakers do not agree on where stress is, therefore the medium-light-heavy theory is hard to confirm. ... In dialects like Mandarin, there is a difference between full syllables, such as le4 ‘happy,’ and weak syllables, such as the aspect marker le (which indicates completion). Full syllables are longer and carry tone. Weak syllables are shorter and usually do not carry tone. Intuitively, full syllables have more stress than weak syllables. ... If we exclude contrastive stress and weak syllables, then it is quite true to say that native speakers can hardly feel stress in Chinese. ... …
sweep_summary: Mandarin (mand1415) is in the catalog as 'lexical' on Duanmu 2000/2011 (open-text grade). Of the 18 title-works with stress in the title, none is a first-hand word-stress description that could be read: the only candidates are Shen 1990 'The Prosody of Mandarin Chinese' (UC Press, print-only: no ebook, not in HathiTrust, PDF of the companion Shen 1986 CLAO article sits behind Persée's altcha) and, less likely, Shen 1991 and Shih 1997 on T3 sandhi (paywalled) and Li Kening 2009 (not located). Four items were downloaded and read in full (Ou 2019, Wang et al. 2020, Arcodia & Montermini 2012 — all silent on Mandarin word stress) plus Yang et al. 2019's abstract; the rest are intonation, discourse, L2 or non-linguistic 'accent' items, or the wrong variety (Chengdu). The best new first-hand statement came from a source already held by the project: Duanmu's 1990 MIT dissertation, sec. 5.1 p. 181 and rule (8) p. 184, which confirms the lexical coding (neutral-tone syllables lexically marked; all regular syllables stressed; relative prominence unclear, Hoa 1983 vs Meredith 1990) but does not supersede Duanmu 2000/2011. An open 2024 Language and Cognition paper (Yu et al.) adds the Chinese-side citations on the disputed Strong-Weak vs Weak-Strong patterns. Tool budgets (web search, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex) ran out mid-search; could not be reached by automated download Benjamins, T&F, AIP, Persée PDF, MUSE and Duanmu's UMich pages. with.

new_statements.quote: Mandarin has two kinds of syllables, stressed and unstressed. Unstressed syllables, also called 'neutral-tone syllables', are toneless and monomoraic, and are mostly marked lexically (Woo 1969, C.Cheng 1973, Chao 1968, H. Lin & Yan 1988). In contrast, stressed syllables, which comprise the overwhelming majority, always have tones and are bimoraic (or sometimes trimoraic finally) in length (cf. Chapter 2). [fn. 1] Among stressed syllables, some may bear greater stress than others. Hoa (1983) suggests that such additional stress is at least partly marked in the lexicon, while Meredith (1990) suggests that it is predictable from the tones of the syllables. My own experience with native Peking Mandarin speakers suggests that while there is never confusion between stressed and unstressed syllables, judgements on the relative prominence of stressed syllables are less clear.
new_statements.citation: Duanmu, San (1990). A Formal Study of Syllable, Tone, Stress and Domain in Chinese Languages. PhD dissertation, MIT.
new_statements.locator: sec. 5.1 'Mandarin', p. 181 (body and fn. 1); stress rules (8) p. 184
new_statements.reading: First-hand, by the same author as the catalog's deciding source but ten years earlier: the stressed/unstressed split coincides with full-tone vs neutral-tone syllables and is a lexical property of the morpheme ('mostly marked lexically'); every regular syllable is stressed (rule (8a) 'Mark all regular syllables', p. 184) and stress domains are left-headed; relative prominence among full syllables is not reliably perceived and is contested (Hoa lexical vs Meredith tone-predictable). This confirms the catalog's 'lexical' kind and its the primary-stress rule/the secondary-stress rule wording.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's lexical kind and with Duanmu 1990 (the existing statement) that the stressed/unstressed split coincides with full vs neutral-tone syllables and is a lexical property; adds that reduced syllables are weak in every environment while full syllables vary by environment, that native speakers cannot rank full syllables for prominence, and DISPUTES the left-headed (initial-prominence) domain detail recorded from Duanmu: Dell finds the arguments for left-headed feet unsupported, the facts compatible with right-headed feet, and cites Chao 1968 and Hoa 1983 for right-edge attraction. Not a different placement claim of Dell's own, so refines rather than contradicts. The p.61…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Beijing Mandarin has two syllable classes: full (bimoraic, tone-bearing) syllables and reduced ('neutral-toned') syllables. Reduced syllables are weakly stressed in every occurrence (a lexical property of the morpheme, distributed like enclitics, never word-initial); full syllables are more prominent than reduced ones, but their prominence relative to one another varies with the environment (morphosyntax, focus) and native speakers cannot reliably rank them. Dell rejects Duanmu's claim that stress is organised in left-headed (initial-prominent) feet: the phonological arguments dissolve and the facts are equally compatible with right-headed feet; he reports (p.53) that Chao (1968) and Hoa (1983) hold that stress is attracted to the right edge of constituents, but offers no alternative placement of his own. Stress in this tone language has mostly indirect cues (p.36).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated as such. Dell notes (p.57) that the difference between full syllables that are weakly stressed by position and reduced syllables is akin to that between secondary-stressed and unstressed syllables in English; Duanmu's system ranks feet so that the initial foot has more stress than the others (p.37, (3b)).
new_statements.exceptions: Reduced (neutral-tone) syllables cannot begin a word (p.57-58); some syllables remain unfooted in Duanmu's derivations; Duanmu's Nonhead Stress makes prominence depend on constituent structure (verb-object vs compound, p.38); Hoa's minimal pair fan1-yi4 shi1-ge1 'translated poem' (fan1 more prominent) vs 'translate poems' (ge1 more prominent) (p.59); Duanmu's corpus count of one-third unstressed toneless syllables refers to Taiwan Standard Chinese (fn.46, p.59).
new_statements.identity_note: Dell 2004 describes Beijing Mandarin ('BM'), explicitly the Beijing-city dialect on which Standard Chinese is based, noting that only a tiny proportion of fluent Standard Chinese speakers are native Beijing speakers (fn. 2, p. 35), and that Duanmu's corpus count of unstressed toneless syllables refers to Standard Chinese as spoken in Taiwan (fn. 46, p. 59). Li 2006 treats standard Mandarin. Pinson & Pinson 2008 (not opened) describes Kunming Hua, a Southwestern Mandarin variety of Yunnan, not Standard/Beijing Mandarin.

new_statements.quote: "Two varieties of Mandarin were included in the study—Guoyu (i.e., Taiwan Mandarin) and Putonghua (i.e., Beijing Mandarin). These two varieties are interesting because among many things, they differ in the existence of lexical stress. Guoyu has almost no lexical stress while Putonghua does. For example, in Putonghua, dong1-xi1 denotes 'east-west' while dong1-xi0 denotes 'thing, stuff'. On the other hand, the two lexical items are homophones (both as dong1-xi1) in Guoyu due to loss of stress contrast." (p. 4; fn. 1: "Tone 0 indicates a neutral tone, which is designated for unstressed syllables.") ... "Since Putonghua makes a distinction between stressed and unstressed syllables, care was taken so that only high tonal targets of stressed Tone 1 and Tone 4 were chosen" (p. 39; fn. 4: "sometimes there is an intermediate level of stress in Putonghua")

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Duanmu 1990 statement (stressed = full-tone syllables, unstressed = neutral-tone syllables, lexically marked): Fon calls it 'lexical stress' and 'stress contrast' and equates Tone 0 / neutral tone with unstressed syllables. It adds (a) an intermediate perceptual stress level in Putonghua and (b) a dialect qualification the catalog lacks: Taiwan Mandarin has nearly lost the contrast. Not about placement; the dissertation itself is on sentence/discourse boundary cues (final lengthening, pause, F0) in English, Guoyu, Putonghua and Japanese.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mandarin is a tone language in which Beijing Putonghua has a lexical stress contrast realised as full-tone (stressed) versus neutral-tone (unstressed, 'Tone 0') syllables, so stress is a lexical property of particular words (dong1-xi1 'east-west' vs dong1-xi0 'thing'); Taiwan Mandarin (Guoyu) has almost no lexical stress, the contrast having been lost. No positional placement rule is given.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Fn. 4 p. 39: the author and Tsan Huang 'noted that sometimes there is an intermediate level of stress in Putonghua', syllables whose tonal contour is fully realised but perceptually less prominent; nothing on secondary stress placement.
new_statements.exceptions: Dialect split: Guoyu (Taiwan Mandarin) has 'almost no lexical stress' / 'loss of stress contrast'; Putonghua keeps it. Tone-digit transcriptions in the scanned came out as 'dong/-xil' / 'dong!-xi0' and were restored to dong1-xi1 / dong1-xi0 from the footnote's Pinyin convention.
new_statements.identity_note: Fon 2002 explicitly separates Guoyu (Taiwan Mandarin) from Putonghua (Beijing Mandarin) and attributes lexical stress only to the latter; its Mandarin statements about stress are about Putonghua. Huang 2004 describes Beijing Putonghua in secs. 2.1 and 4.1.1 and additionally the Rugao (Jiangsu) and Yantai (Shandong) Mandarin dialects in ch. 4, which are not the standard variety; only the Putonghua passages are quoted. The catalog's existing Duanmu 1990 statement is likewise about Standard (Beijing-based) Mandarin.

new_statements.quote: "Sometimes, people also talk about a \"fifth\" tone, namely the neutral tone, whose pitch varies dependent on its preceding tone. There are a few monosyllabic morphemes that are probably inherently neutral-toned, or toneless, such as the tense-aspect marker /le/." (p. 25) ... "Yip (1980) and Zhang (1988) mention that the T214 sandhi is conditioned by the metrical pattern of the utterance and that the T214 that undergoes the sandhi has to be in the weak branch of the stress matrix ... the first T214 in /xiao3jie3/ 'miss' (with a weak-strong pattern) would undergo the T214 sandhi and surface as [xiao35.jie0], whereas that in /jie214.jie214/ 'older sister' (with a strong-weak pattern) would not ... But see Shih (1997), where she holds that stress does not play a role in the sandhi processes." (fn. 7, p. 34) ... "in addition to stress related neutralization rules, Putonghua (or Standard Mandarin) has only one obligatory category-changing process involving normal stressed syllables, namely the T214 sandhi" (p. 86)

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's lexical account and the existing Duanmu 1990 statement (neutral-tone = unstressed, full-tone = stressed, lexically marked). Adds: neutral tone arises both inherently and by stress-related neutralization; lexical SW vs WS patterns in disyllables interact with T3 sandhi (contested). A tone-perception dissertation, so stress is only incidental; no placement rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Putonghua is a four-tone language; a neutral ('fifth') tone marks toneless, unstressed syllables (some morphemes such as /le/ inherently so, others by 'stress related neutralization'), while 'normal stressed syllables' carry full tones. Disyllabic words are cited with lexically given strong-weak (jie3jie 'older sister') or weak-strong (xiao3jie3 'miss') patterns; the work reports, without committing to it, the claim that third-tone sandhi applies only in the metrically weak position. No general placement rule is stated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None stated. Reports Chao's remark that the middle syllable of a trisyllabic phrase is 'relatively weak' (p. 29-30, T35 sandhi).
new_statements.exceptions: Disagreement in the literature on whether stress conditions T3 sandhi (Yip 1980, Zhang 1988 vs Shih 1997); the author 'chose not to commit.. to any particular phonological framework'. The other two dialects treated (Rugao, Yantai) are not the mand1415 standard variety.

Huang 2004 describes Beijing Putonghua in secs. 2.1 and 4.1.1 and additionally the Rugao (Jiangsu) and Yantai (Shandong) Mandarin dialects in ch. 4, which are not the standard variety; only the Putonghua passages are quoted. new_statements.quote: Unlike PTH the neutral tone in KMH consistently has the pitch value of mid-level (i.e. 33). It looks like Tone 1 except it is usually in the context where a neutral tone would be expected (i.e. unstressed syllables). For example, when a familial title is reduplicated the second syllable loses its original tone. [p. 25] ... Gui (1990) also gives some examples where the tone of 头 [tʰəw] doesn't neutralize. In these cases the syllable [tʰəw] is stressed and it seems to still carry its primary semantic meaning of 'head'. ... In KMH the word 首 [səw] is also used as a suffix the way 头 [tʰəw] is used. As a suffix it is not stressed and its tone is neutralized. [p. 26]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Duanmu 1990 statement (stressed = full-tone vs unstressed = neutral-tone syllables, a lexical/morphological property, no placement rule among full syllables) and adds dialect detail: in Kunming (Southwestern Mandarin) the unstressed/neutral-tone syllable has a constant mid-level 33 pitch, with the same morphological loci (reduplicant second syllables, suffixes, particles). It describes the Kunming dialect, not Beijing/Standard Mandarin, though it contrasts the two throughout.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kunming Hua is described as a four-tone language (Tone 1 = 33, Tone 2 = 42, Tone 3 = 55, Tone 4 = 312, with Tone 1 and Tone 3 sandhi). Stress enters only through the stressed/unstressed syllable split familiar from Putonghua: unstressed syllables carry the neutral tone (in KMH realised as a fixed mid-level 33 rather than the context-dependent Putonghua neutral tone) and are the second syllables of reduplicated kin terms and verbs, noun suffixes (头, 首, 子) and particles (了); a morpheme like 头 keeps its full tone when it is stressed and carries its lexical meaning 'head'. No rule for the placement of word stress among full-toned syllables is given; sec. 3.4 notes only a falling (declining) intonation at word and sentence level.
new_statements.exceptions: The noun suffix 子 [-tsɿ] 'often carries Tone 3' rather than the neutral tone and surfaces as [51] utterance-finally (p. 27); 头 does not neutralise in 狗头 'dog's head', 手头 'at hand' where it is stressed (p. 26); particle 了 can itself be stressed and lengthened, then pronounced [la] (pp. 8-9).
new_statements.identity_note: Pinson & Pinson 2008 describes Kunming Hua (昆明话), the Southwestern Mandarin (西南官话) dialect of Kunming, Yunnan, explicitly contrasted with Putonghua; its tone values (33/42/55/312) and its fixed mid-level neutral tone are Kunming facts, not Beijing/Standard Mandarin facts. The other four works concern Standard Mandarin syntax.

tone_statements.citation: Chen, Yiya; Guo, Li. 2022. Zhushan Mandarin. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 52(2): 309-327 (Illustrations of the IPA; online 2020).
tone_statements.quote: Zhushan Mandarin has four lexical tones, marked here with the numerical superscripts 1–4 representing the four tonal categories. … Generally speaking, Tone1 and Tone3 both show a dipping f0 contour but are realized in different registers: T1 within the lower register and T3 within the higher one. … Both T2 and T4 are realized with a falling f0 contour with T2 showing a shallow falling slope and T4 a much steeper fall. … the tone letters, to provide a numerical impression of the f0 contours of the lexical tones: T1 (324), T2 (54), T3 (435), and T4 (51).
tone_statements.locator: pp. 311-312, section 'Lexical tone'
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source
tone_statements.summary: Four lexical tones, one per syllable: T1 324 low dipping, T2 54 high shallow fall, T3 435 high dipping, T4 51 steep fall, with F0 tracks; neutral tone on unstressed syllables; right-dominant sandhi.

tone_statements.quote: Earlier impressionistic descriptions of the dialect (Zhang, Chen & Cheng 1993, Liu 1997) distinguish four citation tones, represented as [24, 41, 55, 31/312] (see Table 1). The first three tones represent a rising, a falling and a high level tone, respectively, but descriptions of the fourth tone vary. … Below, we will provisionally take the fourth tone to be L, assuming a symmetrical four-way system LH, HL, H and L, adopting the representations of tonal phonology (Goldsmith 1976, Duanmu 2007).
tone_statements.locator: p. 2 (FirstView), Section 1 Introduction, last paragraph before Table 2
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source
tone_statements.summary: Kaifeng Mandarin has four lexical syllabic tones: rising LH [24], falling HL [41], high H [55], low L [31/312]; L is longest, often creaky, dipping or falling by speaker; sandhi L.L>LH.L, H.H>HL.H.

tone_statements.citation: Davison, Deborah S. (1992). Parametric variation in pitch realization of 'neutral tone' syllables in Mandarin. In Proceedings of the 18th Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society, February 14-17, 1992. Special Session on the Typology of Tone Languages. Berkeley Linguistic Society 18S. pp. 67-79.
tone_statements.quote: In Mandarin Chinese, most syllables are underlyingly fully specified for tone … The most obvious exceptions are so-called ‘neutral tone’ morphemes or syllables, stressless syllables of words and phrases which lack a lexically contrastive tone. … across two mutually intelligible varieties of Mandarin dialect, both with four lexical tones. … Mandarin’s four lexical tones thus are describable as Tl 55 high level, T2 35 high rising, T3 214 low dipping, and T4 41 falling.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 68-69, Introduction
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source
tone_statements.summary: Four lexical tones (55, 35, 214, 41); neutral-tone syllables are stressless and toneless, given pitch by default mid tone (Taiwan) or interpolation/spreading/default low (North); T3 = L + floating H.

tone_statements.citation: Yip, Moira Jean. 1980. The tonal phonology of Chinese. PhD dissertation, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Dept. of Linguistics and Philosophy. 372 leaves. (Published 1990, New York: Garland.)
tone_statements.quote: Most morphemes in Mandarin carry one of four lexical tones [...]: ma 'mother' First tone. 55 high level; ma 'hemp' Second tone. 35 high rising; ma 'horse' Third tone. 214 low, with rise pre-pausally, 21 low level elsewhere; ma 'to scold' Fourth tone. 41 falling. However, a small number of morphemes never show up with any of these tones, but are always in what is called 'neutral tone'. Phonetically this means that the pitch of such morphemes is predictable from the tone of the preceding morpheme [...]. Dell 2004 (p. 61) concludes that all of PSC's phonological arguments for left-headed feet dissolve under examination, that the distribution of neutral-tone syllables is equally compatible with right-headed feet (Xiamen shows enclitic reduced syllables with right-headed feet, p. 58), and he reports (p. 53) Chao 1968 and Hoa 1983 as holding that stress is attracted to the right edge of constituents; he offers no placement of his own. sources.quote: It is well-known that stress in Chinese is hard to feel. ... Chao (1968: 35) suggests that in a string of full syllables, the last has most stress, the first has slightly less, and the rest have still less. This is known as the ‘medium-light-heavy’ theory. However, as Chao (1968: 38) acknowledges, Mandarin speakers do not agree on where stress is, therefore the medium-light-heavy theory is hard to confirm. ... In dialects like Mandarin, there is a difference between full syllables, such as le4 ‘happy,’ and weak syllables, such as the aspect marker le (which indicates completion). Full syllables are longer and carry tone. Weak syllables are shorter and usually do not carry tone. Intuitively, full syllables have more stress than weak syllables. ... If we exclude contrastive stress and weak syllables, then it is quite true to say that native speakers can hardly feel stress in Chinese. ... …

sources.quote: Mandarin has two kinds of syllables, stressed and unstressed. Unstressed syllables, also called 'neutral-tone syllables', are toneless and monomoraic, and are mostly marked lexically (Woo 1969, C.Cheng 1973, Chao 1968, H. Lin & Yan 1988). In contrast, stressed syllables, which comprise the overwhelming majority, always have tones and are bimoraic (or sometimes trimoraic finally) in length (cf. Chapter 2). [fn. 1:] Among stressed syllables, some may bear greater stress than others. Hoa (1983) suggests that such additional stress is at least partly marked in the lexicon, while Meredith (1990) suggests that it is predictable from the tones of the syllables.

sources.quote: In addition, Mandarin has a neutral tone that signals an unstressed syllable and always occurs in the final syllable of a word. ... Mandarin disyllabic words have two stress patterns, namely, the Strong-Weak and the Weak-Strong pattern (Lu, 1984; Yin, 1982). ... Some researchers believe that both Strong-Weak and Weak-Strong patterns are equally common in Mandarin, while others argued that the Strong-Weak pattern is predominant (Wang & Feng, 2006). There are also researchers considering that the Weak-Strong pattern is the principal pattern (Lin et al., 1984; Xu, 1982), although it is argued that there is no fixed stress pattern in Mandarin (Liu, 2007; Zhou, 2018).
sources.locator: Introduction (online HTML, pp. 1135-1136)
sources.note: OA full text read (Introduction). Second-hand summary of the Chinese-language literature: neutral tone marks an unstressed syllable and 'always occurs in the final syllable of a word'; among full-toned disyllables there are Strong-Weak and Weak-Strong patterns and the literature is contradictory on which predominates (Wang & Feng 2006: SW; Lin, Yan & Sun 1984, Xu 1982: WS; Liu 2007, Zhou 2018: no fixed pattern). Refines the catalog's 'disputed relative prominence' note with the Chinese-side citations; consistent with lexical coding.

sources.tag: read: states tone
sources.quote: The tone system of Mandarin Chinese is commonly described as having four lexical tones, namely high level (T1), rising (T2), dipping/low (T3), and falling (T4), plus one neutral or floating tone, whose shape depends on the preceding tone (Chao 1968). || This study investigated variation in the f0 contours of disyllabic words with the rise-fall (RF) tonal pattern in Taiwan Mandarin. [...] In standard analyses of tone in Mandarin, the rising tone of the first syllable and the falling tone of the second syllable of RF words are inherited from the single-syllable constituents and are taken to be basic, underlying tones. Deviations from these tones are explained by appealing to articulatory and prosodic constraints governing how tones can be realized. Our hypothesis adds word meaning as a missing player in the articulatory arena by arguing that meaning co-determines the realization of Mandarin tones.

sources.quote: Mandarin has four full lexical tones, which are reported to have typical pitch values of High (Tone 1), Rising (Tone 2), Dipping/Low (Tone 3), and Falling (Tone 4). Following the tradition of a five-level scale notion (Chao, 1968), the pitch targets of the four tones are transcribed as [55], [35], [214]/[21], and [51] ... The Tone 3 sandhi (T3S) refers to the process where Tone 3 becomes rising [35] when it precedes another Tone 3. ... The foot is the obligatory domain for T3S. Failing to apply the rule within a foot yields unacceptable readings in any style and at any speech rate. The utterance is the upper boundary of the sandhi rule, across which T3S application is prohibited. At the intermediate levels (superfoot, phrase), T3S applies optionally across feet in an utterance.

Figure 6 shows the RFT analysis of counting from one to seven in Mandarin Chinese by a female adult, in Pinyin transcription yī èr sān sì wŭ liù qī, with high, fall, high, fall, fall–rise (dipping), fall and high lexical tones (i.e. Tones 1, 4, 1, 4, 3, 4, 1).

sources.quote: Mandarin has four citation tones (labeled in this paper as H[igh], R[ising], L[ow], and F[alling]). The Low tone is sometimes pronounced as (or very similar to-see Endnote 2) a Rising tone instead. Specifically, when two Low tones occur next to each other within the same intonational unit, the first one becomes Rising-for example, /niL/ (你, "you") is pronounced with a Low tone, but /niL haoL/ (你好, "hello" [literally "you good"]) is actually pronounced as [niR haoL], with a Rising tone on the first syllable. (The above is a simplified overview of what happens in this particular tonal alternation pattern, known as "third tone sandhi.") [p. 2] ... Note that the Low-tone syllables used the full (falling-rising) contour of the Low tone, which generally only occurs when the syllable is pronounced in isolation or at the end of an intonational phrase, rather than the arguably more common low-falling contour which results from "half-third" sandhi when a Low-tone syllable occurs before any non-Low-tone syllable in the same intonational phrase. sources.quote: There are four lexical tones in Tianjin Mandarin. [...] Tone 1 is a low-register falling tone, with a pitch contour that falls from the middle to the lower end of the speaker's pitch range. Tone 2 is a high-register rising tone, whose pitch contour rises from the middle to the upper end of the pitch range. Tone 3 is a low-register dipping tone, which falls slightly from the lower pitch range, stays at the bottom and then rises to the mid pitch range of the speaker. Tone 4 is a high-register falling tone which falls from the upper end to the mid pitch range. (p. 124) [...] four disyllabic tone sandhi rules [...] (1) T1+T1 (L+L) -> T3+T1 (LH+L) (2) T3+T3 (LH+LH) -> T2+T3 (H+LH) (3) T4+T4 (HL+HL) -> T1+T4 (L+HL) (4) T4+T1 (HL+L) -> T2+T1 (H+L) (p. 125) [...] we confirmed three tonal sequences with tone sandhi changes: (1) two low-falling tones (T1T1), (2) a high-falling tone followed by a low-falling tone (T4T1), and (3) two low-dipping tones (T3T3). [...] no tonal neutralization was observed over any of the sandhi processes. Rather, we argue that T3T3 is a near-merger sandhi case, while T1T1 and T4T1 can be classified as no-merger sandhi sequences. (p. 123)

sources.quote: Mandarin is a “lexical tone language” (Yip, 2002, p. 2) with four tones (e.g., Bauer & Benedict, 1997; Duanmu, 2004; Hashimoto, 1972) that are typically described in terms of Chao's (1930) tone letters, which range from 1 (low pitch, or F0, within the speaker's range) to 5 (high F0): High level [55] (Tone 1; hereafter, T1), mid rising [35] (Tone 2; T2), falling rising [214] (Tone 3; T3), and high falling [51] (Tone 4; T4) (see Figure 1a, top left). For example, /ta55/ `carry', /ta35/ `reach', /ta214/ `hit', and /ta51/ `large' are all meaningfully different words solely because of their lexical tone differences (minimal tone contrasts).

sources.quote: Most morphemes in Mandarin carry one of four lexical tones [...]: ma 'mother' First tone. 55 high level; ma 'hemp' Second tone. 35 high rising; ma 'horse' Third tone. 214 low, with rise pre-pausally, 21 low level elsewhere; ma 'to scold' Fourth tone. 41 falling. However, a small number of morphemes never show up with any of these tones, but are always in what is called 'neutral tone'. Phonetically this means that the pitch of such morphemes is predictable from the tone of the preceding morpheme [...]. [p. 283:] If this is right, then the four tones of Mandarin may be represented as follows: [+ Upper] 55 H H; [+ Upper] 35 L H; [- Upper] 21 L L; [+ Upper] 51 H L.
sources.locator: sec. 1.2.1 'Mandarin Suffixes', p. 79 (obvious misreads 'rna'/'Fuurth'/'nunlber' corrected to ma/Fourth/number); sec. 5.1 'Mandarin', p. 283
sources.note: Four lexical tones 55, 35, 214 (21 non-prepausally), 41/51 plus toneless 'neutral tone' morphemes whose pitch is predictable from the preceding tone; tones decomposed into register feature [+/-Upper] and two tonemes (H/L) each: 55 = [+U] HH, 35 = [+U] LH, 21(4) = [-U] LL, 51 = [+U] HL; third-tone sandhi analysed as register dissimilation; neutral tone = deletion of tonemes on metrically weak (non-branching) syllables.

tone.quote: In Mandarin Chinese, most syllables are underlyingly fully specified for tone … The most obvious exceptions are so-called ‘neutral tone’ morphemes or syllables, stressless syllables of words and phrases which lack a lexically contrastive tone. … across two mutually intelligible varieties of Mandarin dialect, both with four lexical tones. … Mandarin’s four lexical tones thus are describable as Tl 55 high level, T2 35 high rising, T3 214 low dipping, and T4 41 falling.
tone.locator: pp. 68-69, Introduction
tone.check: quotation verified in source
tone.summary: Four lexical tones (55, 35, 214, 41); neutral-tone syllables are stressless and toneless, given pitch by default mid tone (Taiwan) or interpolation/spreading/default low (North); T3 = L + floating H.
tone.says: Four lexical tones (55, 35, 214, 41); neutral-tone syllables are stressless and toneless, given pitch by default mid tone (Taiwan) or interpolation/spreading/default low (North); T3 = L + floating H.
